short: Anglo-French war that opened the Chinese interior and burned the Summer Palace.
full:
On 8 October 1856 Qing officers boarded the Arrow at Canton, a Chinese-owned lorcha whose British registration had lapsed, and arrested its crew. Britain treated the boarding as an insult to the flag; France joined after a missionary was executed in Guangxi. The Qing were already fighting the Taiping in the south and had little to spare. Canton fell in December 1857, the Taku forts guarding the approach to Tianjin followed, and in June 1858 the court signed the Treaties of Tientsin, then declined to ratify them.

An expedition of some 18,000 British and French troops returned in 1860, took the Taku forts in August and marched on Peking. After envoys sent under a flag of truce were tortured and killed, Lord Elgin ordered the Old Summer Palace destroyed; the burning began on 18 October and lasted three days. The Convention of Peking of 24 October ceded Kowloon to Britain, opened Tianjin, admitted resident foreign legations and missionaries inland, and legalised the trade the first Opium War had been fought over. Russia, mediating, took the land north of the Amur and founded Vladivostok.
